title: I’m a software engineer of 5 years looking to make cozy 2D pixel games. Which tools/resources should I be looking at?
author: rainyengineer
selftext:
I’ve always wanted to make games and now I’d like to give it a try. I have lots of different game ideas to try out. My genre is the cozy pixel vibe like Stardew or Graveyard Keeper. 

From what I’ve gathered, it would probably be helpful to pick up a Claude Pro sub and use Godot + godot-ai, and asperite. Does this around about right? Is there anything else I should use to get started? 

I’ll take any advice you guys have for me!

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: Sure. Just give it a go

comments.author: fyndor
comments.body: Yep.  LDTK or Tiled for level editing (prefer LDTK)

replies.author: BenTheSodaman
replies.body:
Started with one myself, but if I get going early in the week, I exhaust the weekly limit during the 3rd day and that's without fully taking advantage of each 5-hour window.

At the time, the choices were 20 USD + pay as you go. Or 200 USD.

And I wasn't using it enough to justify the 200 USD yet.

So a second subscription for another 20 USD seemed more feasible at the time.

———

Hypothetically, if I didn't have a subscription and had done a pay-as-you-go all the way through, the usage spreadsheet on day 16 suggests I would have spent 190+ USD by that point.

For the way and frequency I use it, a x2.5 allowance plan would fit my needs. So my compromise at the time was two subscriptions at 20 USD. (even though now the x5 allowance plans for 100 USD now exist.)

replies.author: Neither_Bluebird_795
replies.body:
So many reasons but the Main reason is budget and limits. 

Here is my workflow 

Claude plans and writes the prompt / code   
GPT reviews it   
Claude makes changes based of reviews  
GPT review one more time   
If good Claude writes the final prompt / code 

Codex executes it (because it’s better and cheaper at this part)

comments.author: nian2326076
comments.body:
Godot is great for 2D games with its flexible script and node system. Aseprite is perfect for pixel art, so you're on the right track. You might also want to try Tiled for map creation—it works well with Godot. Check out Godot's community and tutorials, as they can be really helpful when you're starting.

If you're getting into AI, Godot's built-in tools are pretty basic. You might want to explore more advanced libraries or write some custom AI scripts. Since you have a software engineering background, scripting and tweaking things should come naturally.

Don't worry about making things perfect at first. Start with a simple project to get comfortable, then build from there. Good luck!

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body:
Using a normal AI model like Claude with Nano Banana or GPT image 2 wont work for 2d animations such as spritesheets, because AI models cant output transparency, and image models alone have no understanding of animation.

That is actually why I built GameLab Studio ([https://gamelabstudio.co](https://gamelabstudio.co)). It’s designed for game assets and it’ll generate consistent pixel-art or any style sprites, animations and full transparent background spritesheets for anything.

https://i.redd.it/v77wf2vdmr0h1.gif

It also enforces consistency across scale, palette, and angles, by using already generated angles of the same asset for reference, so you don’t end up with “AI asset soup” during prototyping.

We also have a seamless tileable edge-aware texture generation model

Gamelabs Studio also has an MCP that plugs right into your agent like Cursor, to enable rapid iteration right in your code editor

[https://gamelabstudio.co/blog/mcp-setup-guide](https://gamelabstudio.co/blog/mcp-setup-guide)

**Gamelabs Studio has been used in real production game releases, like** [https://www.crazygames.com/game/age-of-steam-tower-defence?bypassCache=hgp3p](https://www.crazygames.com/game/age-of-steam-tower-defence?bypassCache=hgp3p)
